fields.h1: Build a Medical History Form Your Clinic Can Search
fields.hero_description: Tell Emergent which answers need a second look. It builds the medical history form patients complete on any device, and the database that holds every answer.
fields.features_heading: What a History Form Does Once It Leaves Paper
fields.features_subheading: Six parts of the form that paper handles badly, each set up from the prompt.
fields.feature_1:
Every answer stored as a field

Save each answer as its own field in the clinic's database, not as a scanned page. Staff can pull every patient who reported asthma or a penicillin allergy without opening a PDF.
fields.feature_2:
Medications in rows, supplements apart

Give each prescription its own row with the dose and the schedule it is taken on. Vitamins and herbal supplements get a question of their own further down the same screen.
fields.feature_3:
Allergies paired with the reaction

Ask what happened beside every allergy entry, such as a rash or trouble breathing. The reaction sits in the row with the drug or food behind it, where a clinician reads both at once.
fields.feature_4:
Family history by relative

Collect conditions for each parent and sibling on their own row, with the age at diagnosis. Answers are stored per relative instead of in one free-text box a nurse has to decode.
fields.feature_5:
A signed statement at the end

Close the form with a statement that the history is complete to the best of the patient's knowledge. Collect a typed or drawn signature, stored on the record with the signing date.
fields.feature_6:
The code goes where you want it

Export the full code for the form and its database to your GitHub repository. A developer can run it on the clinic's own servers or connect it to any clinic system with an API.

fields.usecase_heading: History Forms for Four Kinds of Care
fields.tab_content_1:
Anesthesia reactions flagged with a week to spare

Ridgeline Surgery Center sends the history link seven days before each procedure. Patients answer the anesthesia questions first, sleep apnea among them. A yes to an earlier reaction to anesthesia sends the case to Dr. Omar Haddad, the anesthesiologist, while there is time to change the plan.
fields.tab_content_2:
Heart disease charted for each relative

Brookfield Heart Clinic asks about heart disease one relative at a time, with the age at diagnosis for each. A father or brother diagnosed before 55, or a mother or sister before 65, adds the new patient to the list Nina Patel, the nurse practitioner, reviews before the first visit.
fields.tab_content_3:
Employers see cleared or follow-up, never the answers

Applicants for warehouse jobs at Globex fill in the history form from Bayview Occupational Health before their pre-placement exam. Dr. Lena Ortiz reviews it inside the clinic's records. The Globex hiring team receives one of two statuses per applicant, Cleared or Follow-up needed, and none of the answers.
fields.tab_content_4:
Answers given in Spanish fill the English fields

The opening screen at Alder Street Clinic lets each patient choose English or Spanish. Every question after it appears in that language, and each checkbox answer saves to the same field in both versions. Dr. Paul Mendes reads a single record in English, with free-text answers kept as the patient wrote them.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Medical History Form
fields.howto_description: The building is quick. The real work is choosing which questions earn a place and which answers a clinician should see before the patient walks in.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Collect the history pages in use
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Order the sections like an exam
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Write the follow-up for every yes
fields.howto_step_1_des: Gather every history page patients fill in today, including the sheet the front desk hands over. Ask each clinician which answers they check before a visit. Keep those questions and cut any that nobody has acted on in the past year.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Open with medications and allergies. Past conditions and surgeries come next, then family history, then tobacco and alcohol use. Immunizations close the form. Give each section its own screen, sized to read on a phone without zooming or scrolling sideways.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Decide what a clinician needs once a patient answers yes. A surgery needs the year and the hospital. A condition needs the year diagnosed and whether it is still treated. Patients who answer no move straight past the follow-up questions.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Pick the answers that need a person before the visit, such as a blood thinner on the medication list or a past problem with anesthesia. Name one staff member for each answer, and choose whether the alert arrives by email or in Slack.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Paste the sections and the alert rules into the prompt in plain English. Emergent builds the form and the database table behind it. When a clinician asks for a new question later, add it with another prompt and the live form updates.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Some patients will still ask for paper. Keep a blank printout at the front desk, and have staff key those answers into the same online form. Every history then sits in one database, whichever way the patient filled it in.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Test it as three made-up patients
fields.howto_step_7_des: Fill in the form on a phone as a healthy adult, as a patient on four medications and as one who reports an anesthesia reaction. Confirm each alert reaches the person you named and that every answer shows up in the right field.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is almost all printable PDFs from health systems and clinics (Memorial Health, UNC Health, a State Department exam form, a family history sheet, Purdue's clinic) plus one downloadable template guide. Each one lists the same sections: medications, allergies, past conditions and surgeries, family history, social history and immunizations. This page names those sections and what to ask in each, then shows four places a history form does more online than on paper: a surgery center that screens for anesthesia problems before the surgery date, a cardiology practice that maps family history by relative, an occupational health clinic that sends the employer a clearance and keeps the answers, and a community clinic that offers the form in English and Spanish.

A cardiology practice asks about heart disease relative by relative, and a parent or sibling diagnosed before 55 puts the patient on the list the nurse practitioner reviews before the first visit.

An occupational health clinic collects a job applicant's health history before a pre-placement exam, and the employer receives only a cleared or follow-up status while the answers stay in the clinic's records.
A community clinic lets each patient choose English or Spanish at the first screen, and every checkbox answer is saved to the same field so the provider reads one record in either language.
